title: Cost-of-living clashes in Brussels and Liege
deck: Belgian students copied France's school blockades, the anger turned to cost of living and governance, and two weekends of street clashes in Brussels now sit inside a wider European protest wave.

fuel.title: Italian and Albanian clashes join the wave
fuel.how: Protests in Rome, Turin, Bologna, Milan and Tirana over costs, education and governance add momentum that Belgian protesters can draw on.

fuel.title: Second Brussels clash; shops boarded up
fuel.how: A week after looting, police and protesters clashed again in Brussels, nine people were arrested and shopkeepers boarded up, which keeps the confrontation alive.

fuel.title: Living-cost anger behind Europe's protests
fuel.how: Coverage ties the demonstrations to the gap between wages and prices, the grievance that turned a school protest into a broader one.

card.headline: Belgium's clashes are a French-style school protest that turned into a cost-of-living and anti-government fight

forYou.line: Shops in central Brussels boarded up on 24 October for fear of a repeat of the previous week's looting. Plan for protest Saturdays.
Expect police cordons and disruption around demonstrations in Brussels. We have no sourced numbers on transport impact.
No sign of a market effect in our sources. The risk is political contagion across Europe, not Belgian finances.
The wave began with school blockades. School-level disruption and tension may continue.
Belgium's interior minister calls it violence, not protest. That framing points to a security-led response, not concessions.

whatHappened: On 17 October 2026, police clashed with demonstrators in Brussels and Liege. It followed weeks of high-school protests that echoed the school blockades in France. Belgium's interior minister called what happened violence, not protest.
A week later, on 24 October, protesters and police clashed again in Brussels. Nine people were arrested. Shops were boarded up because of fears of a repeat of the previous week's looting.

The Belgian wave is part of a bigger pattern. Reports from 24 and 25 October describe clashes with police in Rome, Turin, Bologna, Milan and Tirana over living costs, education and governance. Several outlets now speak of a protest wave across France, Italy, Belgium and Albania.
whyItMatters: Politics and protest: this is a copycat. French students blockaded schools over teacher shortages. Belgian students copied the tactic and the demands weeks later. That means unrest travels fast between neighbouring countries, and one country's school dispute can become another's street fight.

Security: two Saturdays of confrontation in the capital of both Belgium and the EU have already changed behaviour. Shops are boarded up and police are bracing for repeat looting. The interior minister's wording suggests the state is treating the events as a public-order problem, which can narrow the room for talks.

Living costs: coverage ties the demonstrations to the gap between wages and prices, and to anger over education and governance. If that grievance is real and widespread, a firm police response will not remove it. That is why the unrest could return.
Scale check: Belgium's severity is lower than France's. The sources we have give no Belgian crowd size or damage figure, so we rate the impact at 2 out of 5.

winners.why: Boarding up and riot-risk worries raise demand for private security and cover (our estimate).
Anti-government anger is a political opening in any country. We have no Belgian polling to size it.

losers.why: Shops were looted on 17 October, and had to board up again by 24 October.
Headlines call the protests anti-government. It has to answer both disorder and cost-of-living complaints.
The interior minister's 'violence, not protest' framing risks lumping them in with looters.

whatsNext: More Saturday marches are plausible. The first two came a week apart, 17 and 24 October.
Watch whether the government offers anything on school funding or living costs, or sticks to a security line.
Watch France and Italy. Belgian unrest has followed French unrest, so what happens there may shape Belgium.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely path for Belgium's protests over the next month?
options: Fades quickly as the school-led wave burns out
Recurring weekend clashes with small arrest numbers
Escalates into nationwide unrest on the French scale
predict.explanation: Our base case is recurring weekend clashes at modest scale, at about 40%. The first two weekends produced violence but, as far as our sources show, small arrest numbers. A fade-out is the next most likely at about 30%.

timeline.title: French students begin school blockades
timeline.detail: Starting in late September, French high-school students blockaded schools over teacher shortages. This is the model Belgian students later copied (see france-unrest-2026).

timeline.title: Belgian high-school protests begin (approximate)
timeline.detail: Our sources say only that Belgian students copied the French blockades weeks before 17 October. The exact start date is not in them, so this entry is placed early in October as an estimate.

timeline.title: Mass marches in France
timeline.detail: About 550,000 marched in France and roughly 2,400 were arrested in one day, the same day as the Belgian clashes (from the connected France dossier).

timeline.title: Police and demonstrators clash in Brussels and Liege
timeline.detail: Belgium's interior minister called it violence, not protest.

timeline.title: Looting in Brussels (date approximate)
timeline.detail: A 24 October headline refers to fears of a repeat of 'last week's looting', which puts it around the 17 October clashes.

timeline.title: Europe-wide cost-of-living framing
timeline.detail: Euronews reports on the economic pressures, wages against prices, behind the protests across Europe.

timeline.title: Second Brussels clash; nine arrests
timeline.detail: Protesters and police clash at anti-government protests. Shops are boarded up in fear of a repeat of the previous week's looting.

timeline.title: Clashes in Italian cities and Tirana
timeline.detail: Protesters clash with police in Rome, Turin, Bologna, Milan and Tirana over living costs, education and governance.

timeline.detail: Outlets describe anger over costs, education and governance across France, Italy, Belgium and Albania.

causes.name: Cost-of-living squeeze
causes.detail: Coverage links the protests to the gap between wages and prices across Europe. We have no Belgian-specific figures.

causes.name: Education grievances
causes.detail: Italian protests were reported as being over education as well as costs. The Belgian wave began with high-school protests that copied French demands on teacher shortages.

causes.name: Distrust of governance
causes.detail: Headlines call the Brussels events anti-government protests and cite political failures as a cause.

causes.name: Copycat school blockades
causes.detail: Belgian students copied French blockades and demands weeks after the French began.

causes.name: Police confrontation
causes.detail: Clashes in Brussels and Liege on 17 October, and again in Brussels on 24 October.

causes.name: Looting and framing
causes.detail: Looting gave the interior minister grounds to call the events violence, not protest, which can sharpen the dispute (our judgement).

causes.name: Cross-border momentum
causes.detail: Clashes in Italian cities and Tirana, and media talk of a wave, keep the movement visible.

stakeholders.name: Belgium's interior minister
stakeholders.role: Responsible for policing and public order
stakeholders.wants: Order restored; the clashes framed as criminal violence
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep a firm security line and push prosecutions for looting and violence

stakeholders.name: High-school and student protesters
stakeholders.wants: Better schools and help with living costs, in line with the demands copied from France
stakeholders.leverage: Numbers, social-media reach, the ability to disrupt schools
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep protesting, but risk being overshadowed by looters and clashes

stakeholders.name: Brussels police and city authorities
stakeholders.wants: Prevent a repeat of the looting; limit damage
stakeholders.leverage: Cordons, arrests, seizing items (they defended seizing swimming goggles at a protest, per a Brussels Times headline)
stakeholders.likelyMove: Heavier presence on protest Saturdays; arrests of those seen as violent

stakeholders.name: Brussels shopkeepers
stakeholders.role: Exposed to looting and lost trade
stakeholders.likelyMove: Board up on protest days; press for security and cover

stakeholders.name: French government
stakeholders.role: Origin of the model; faces the larger unrest
stakeholders.leverage: Whatever it concedes sets expectations across the border
stakeholders.likelyMove: Depends on how its own crisis develops; see france-unrest-2026

stakeholders.name: Italian and Albanian protesters and governments
stakeholders.role: Parallel movements in the same wave
stakeholders.wants: Action on costs, education and governance
stakeholders.leverage: Same shared narrative of a European protest wave
stakeholders.likelyMove: Further protests; their size will shape the narrative around Belgium

sectors.sector: Retail and hospitality in central Brussels
sectors.why: Looting around 17 October and boarding up on 24 October mean lost trade and costs. We have no figures.
Demand for guarding and riot cover is likely to rise (our estimate).
The protests began in high schools. Disruption hurts teaching, but the pressure may bring attention and funding (judgement).
Heavier deployments on protest days and a political push for tough enforcement.

sectors.sector: Events, tourism and transport in Brussels
sectors.why: Protest days disrupt the city centre. Low confidence; our sources give no data.
Anti-government anger pressures the government. Whether the opposition benefits is unclear without polling.

dailyLife.effect: Shops were boarded up on 24 October for fear of a repeat of looting.
Expect police presence and arrests; nine were detained on 24 October. We have no sourced transport detail.
The protests are tied in coverage to the gap between wages and prices across Europe.
The wave began with high-school protests copied from France; further blockades are possible.

scenarios.name: Recurring weekend clashes
scenarios.looksLike: Saturday protests in Brussels continue with small arrest numbers, shops board up, and the government stays on a security line.
signposts: Arrest totals remain in the tens
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Belgium stays a sideshow to France and Italy, but a steady source of images that feed the European protest narrative.

scenarios.name: Fade-out
scenarios.looksLike: The school-led energy runs down, protests shrink, and the looting does not repeat.
signposts: Fewer arrests on the next protest day
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The Belgian episode is remembered as a copycat that did not take root.

scenarios.name: Escalation
scenarios.looksLike: Larger marches, wider damage, curfews or bans on demonstrations.
signposts: Unions or other groups join the students
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Belgium joins France as a major case, and EU institutions in Brussels face unrest on their doorstep.

scenarios.name: Concession reset
scenarios.looksLike: The government announces money for schools or help with living costs and talks open with student groups.
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Calmer streets, a modest budget cost, and an example other governments may follow.

predictions.text: Further protests with clashes will take place in Brussels at least once more before the end of November 2026.
Belgium will not see unrest on the French scale: no single day will exceed several thousand arrests.
The government will not abandon its 'violence, not protest' framing, and will announce no major new living-cost package aimed at protesters before year-end.
Unrest will continue in at least two other European countries besides Belgium and France during November 2026.
Reporting will still describe a linked protest wave across France, Italy and Belgium in January 2027.

actions: Plan for boarding up and early closing on protest Saturdays in central Brussels.
Check insurance for riot and looting cover.
Brief staff on routes and safety around demonstrations.
Treat this as political contagion risk, not a Belgian financial event; our sources show no market effect.
Watch the French situation, which is the bigger driver.
Check police and city notices before travelling into central Brussels on Saturdays.
Parents should watch school communications for blockades or disruption.
Separate prosecution of looting from engagement with students' grievances.
Address the wages-and-prices complaint directly, since a security response alone will not remove it.
Coordinate with neighbouring governments on a shared pattern.

analogues.whatFollowed: Several nights of violence and thousands of arrests, with no major policy change. Disorder tends to fade under heavy policing while the grievances remain.
A French fuel-tax protest spread to other countries, including Belgium, and faded in most of them. A cost-of-living grievance can cross borders quickly.
Rising bills prompted protests in several countries and relief packages from governments. Concessions on living costs were a common response.

watch.title: Next Saturday in Brussels
watch.why: The first two clashes were a week apart; a third would suggest a pattern, a quiet day a fade-out.

watch.title: Government response on schools and living costs

watch.title: Arrest and damage totals
watch.why: Our sources give only the nine arrests on 24 October. Larger counts would show escalation.

watch.title: Italy and Albania
watch.why: Continued clashes in Rome, Turin, Bologna, Milan and Tirana keep the wave in the headlines.

watch.title: France
watch.why: Belgian unrest followed French unrest, so French developments are the best leading signal (see france-unrest-2026).

watch.title: Protest bans or curfews in Brussels
watch.why: These would mark a step up in the state's response.

evidence.method: Drafted from the five listed sources, a set of wire headlines matched to the event, the event summary and the connected France dossier. We did not read full articles for most items, so facts are limited to what the headlines and the summary state. No Belgian crowd sizes, damage totals or polling were available. Scenario probabilities, sector impacts, daily-life effects and analogues are the author's estimates and are flagged as such.
